title: Building a missing feature: how a new word gets into Omega
summary: Drake's rule: if .om doesn't have a feature you need, make that feature. No host-language helper passed off as Omega. I'll walk you through a real addition, the random host word (Linux getrandom): keyword id 135, the hrand lowering in omc.om, one OMEGESE row, a host gate fixture that can fail, refusal codes, a corpus audit and a new compiler fixpoint, all in one commit.
goal: Turn a missing capability into a proposal and a complete, gated word addition, using the random host word as the model.
key_steps: Write the proposal: need, word, types, result convention
List the refusals (compile codes) and run-time traps
Add the keyword and the lowering in seed/omc/omc.om
Add a gate fixture that can fail and a negative control
Update OMEGESE and the guide, audit the corpus for the newly reserved word, rebuild the fixpoint

example.code:
note kwpack.om: how omc spells a keyword inside itself. The bytes of "random", first byte lowest,
note packed into one ulong: the number fn kw in seed/omc/omc.om compares against for word id 135
text word "random"
fn putnum v ulong to long
note write v in decimal and a newline. A ulong has at most 20 digits, so bound 20 is proved
d = new uchar 21 0
o = new uchar 21 0
n = ulong 0
x = v
while true bound 20
put d n uchar add rem x 10 48
n = add n 1
x = div x 10
if eq x 0
break
end
end
for i ulong n
put o i get d sub sub n i 1
end
put o n 10
w = write 1 o 0 add n 1
ret w
end
fn main to int
v = ulong 0
for i ulong len word
v = or v shl ulong get word i mul i 8
end
w = putnum v
ret 0
end

common_mistake: Filling the gap with a C, Rust, Python or shell helper and calling it Omega, or landing a word without refusal cases, a fixture that can fail, a guide row and a corpus audit for the newly reserved spelling. If you cannot land it, file the concrete proposal instead.
evidence_note: The random word, its host fixture (and a mutated copy that must fail) and its refusals run on Linux AArch64 with omc befb8199...8a1d; reproduced byte for byte (random bytes are never printed). The extension workflow is a project rule; no new word was added by this lesson.
